claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the blastomere isolation data.

claims.claim: Cell-type-specific variation in cytokinesis failure upon forminCYK-1 disruption is controlled cell-extrinsically in EMS.
claims.source: These results suggest that cell-type-specific variation in cytokinesis failure upon forminCYK-1 disruption is controlled cell-intrinsically in P2 and cell-extrinsically in EMS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the blastomere isolation data.

claims.claim: All paired blastomeres from control embryos successfully completed cytokinesis after temperature upshift to restrictive temperature.
claims.source: After temperature upshift to restrictive temperature, all paired blastomeres from control embryos successfully completed cytokinesis, and all paired ABd-ABd blastomeres from formincyk-1(ts) mutant embryos failed to divide, as expected (Figure 7B,C; Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B,C and Video 4.

claims.claim: All paired ABd-ABd blastomeres from formincyk-1(ts) mutant embryos failed to divide after temperature upshift to restrictive temperature.
claims.source: After temperature upshift to restrictive temperature, all paired blastomeres from control embryos successfully completed cytokinesis, and all paired ABd-ABd blastomeres from formincyk-1(ts) mutant embryos failed to divide, as expected (Figure 7B,C; Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B,C and Video 4.

claims.claim: In EMS-P2 paired blastomeres from formincyk-1(ts) mutants, 29% of P2 cells divided successfully (9/31 P2 cells complete cytokinesis).
claims.source: In EMS-P2 paired blastomeres from formincyk-1(ts) mutants, 29% of P2 cells divided successfully (9/31 P2 cells complete cytokinesis), similar to isolated P2 blastomeres (Figures 6D and 7C; Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6D and 7C and Video 4.

claims.claim: 16% of EMS blastomeres in paired EMS-P2 doublets from formincyk-1(ts) mutants divided successfully (5/31 EMS cells complete cytokinesis).
claims.source: Furthermore, 16% of EMS blastomeres in paired EMS-P2 doublets divided successfully (5/31 EMS cells complete cytokinesis) (Figure 7B,C), in contrast to isolated EMS blastomeres (Figure 6D) or manually paired EMS-ABd blastomeres (0/15 EMS cells complete cytokinesis), which never divided successfully (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claims.claim: Isolated EMS blastomeres or manually paired EMS-ABd blastomeres from formincyk-1(ts) mutants never divided successfully (0/15 EMS cells complete cytokinesis).
claims.source: Furthermore, 16% of EMS blastomeres in paired EMS-P2 doublets divided successfully (5/31 EMS cells complete cytokinesis) (Figure 7B,C), in contrast to isolated EMS blastomeres (Figure 6D) or manually paired EMS-ABd blastomeres (0/15 EMS cells complete cytokinesis), which never divided successfully (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Direct cell-cell contact from P2 is sufficient to mediate protection against cytokinesis failure in EMS.
claims.source: Thus, direct cell-cell contact from P2 is sufficient to mediate protection against cytokinesis failure in EMS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the blastomere pairing data.

claims.claim: In formincyk-1(ts) paired EMS-P2 doublets in which the EMS cell divided successfully, there was a significantly larger cell-cell contact area compared to in doublets in which the EMS cell failed in cytokinesis (p=0.0266).
claims.source: In formincyk-1(ts) paired EMS-P2 doublets in which the EMS cell divided successfully, there was a significantly larger cell-cell contact area compared to in doublets in which the EMS cell failed in cytokinesis (p=0.0266; Supplementary file 1; Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in cell-cell contact area between paired doublets from control embryos and paired doublets from formincyk-1(ts) mutants in which EMS divided successfully (p=0.3056).
claims.source: There was no significant difference in cell-cell contact area between paired doublets from control embryos and paired doublets from formincyk-1(ts) mutants in which EMS divided successfully (p=0.3056; Supplementary file 1; Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Increased cell-cell contact area correlated with an increased probability of successful EMS division.
claims.source: Because increased cell-cell contact area correlated with an increased probability of successful EMS division and because P2 to EMS signaling is dependent on cell-cell contact, this result suggests a correlation between successful P2 to EMS signaling and successful EMS division when forminCYK-1 activity is reduced.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the cell-cell contact area data.

claims.claim: There is a correlation between successful P2 to EMS signaling and successful EMS division when forminCYK-1 activity is reduced.
claims.source: Because increased cell-cell contact area correlated with an increased probability of successful EMS division and because P2 to EMS signaling is dependent on cell-cell contact, this result suggests a correlation between successful P2 to EMS signaling and successful EMS division when forminCYK-1 activity is reduced.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the cell-cell contact area data and knowledge about P2 to EMS signaling.

claims.claim: Spindle orientation in EMS cells is a marker for successful P2-EMS signaling.
claims.source: Another marker for successful P2-EMS signaling is spindle orientation in EMS cells.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about P2-EMS signaling.

claims.claim: During extrinsic P2 to EMS cell-fate signaling, receptor tyrosine kinase (MES-1) and WntMOM-2 from P2 activate SrcSRC-1 and FrizzledMOM-5 proteins/receptors in EMS to promote differential cell fate specification and proper spindle orientation during the asymmetric EMS cell division.
claims.source: During extrinsic P2 to EMS cell-fate signaling, receptor tyrosine kinase (MES-1) and WntMOM-2 from P2 activate SrcSRC-1 and FrizzledMOM-5 proteins/receptors in EMS to promote differential cell fate specification and proper spindle orientation during the asymmetric EMS cell division (Figure 8A) (Goldstein, 1992, 1993, 1995a, 1995b; Rocheleau et al., 1997; Thorpe et al., 1997; Bei et al., 2002; Arata et al., 2010; Schierenberg, 1987; Heppert et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In EMS-P2 doublets isolated from control embryos, the EMS spindle always aligned near the doublet axis (~180°), indicating successful P2 to EMS cell-fate signaling.
claims.source: In EMS-P2 doublets isolated from control embryos, which always divided successfully, the EMS spindle always aligned near the doublet axis (~180°), indicating successful P2 to EMS cell-fate signaling (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: In formincyk-1(ts) EMS-P2 doublets, EMS spindle orientation varied widely relative to the doublet axis with only 48% of formincyk-1(ts) EMS spindles in alignment with the EMS-P2 doublet axis (>160° relative to the EMS-P2 doublet axis) (15/31 EMS cells).
claims.source: In formincyk-1(ts) EMS-P2 doublets, EMS spindle orientation varied widely relative to the doublet axis with only 48% of formincyk-1(ts) EMS spindles in alignment with the EMS-P2 doublet axis (>160° relative to the EMS-P2 doublet axis) (15/31 EMS cells; Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The spindle orientation data suggests a potential role for forminCYK-1 in the F-actin-dependent P2 to EMS signaling event.
claims.source: This result suggests a potential role for forminCYK-1 in this F-actin-dependent P2 to EMS signaling event (Goldstein, 1995b).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the spindle orientation data and a citation to Goldstein, 1995b.

claims.claim: In formincyk-1(ts) EMS cells that successfully completed cytokinesis, the EMS spindle axis was always aligned with the doublet axis (5/5 EMS cells).
claims.source: In contrast, in formincyk-1(ts) EMS cells that successfully completed cytokinesis, the EMS spindle axis was always aligned with the doublet axis (Figure 8C), consistent with successful P2 to EMS signaling (5/5 EMS cells) (Bei et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and a citation to Bei et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Of the paired formincyk-1(ts) EMS cells with normal spindle alignment, 33% (5/15 EMS cells) divided successfully, a similar frequency to that observed in intact embryos.
claims.source: Indeed, of the paired formincyk-1(ts) EMS cells with normal spindle alignment, 33% (5/15 EMS cells; Figure 8C) divided successfully, a similar frequency to that observed in intact embryos.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Cytokinesis outcome in P2 was independent of EMS spindle orientation and thus P2-EMS cell-fate signaling.
claims.source: Consistent with the cell-intrinsic regulation of cytokinesis in P2, cytokinesis outcome in P2 was independent of EMS spindle orientation and thus P2-EMS cell-fate signaling (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Srcsrc-1(RNAi) decreased the frequency of successful division in EMS (2/46 cells) compared with control(RNAi) (21/65 cells complete cytokinesis) in formincyk-1(ts) mutant embryos.
claims.source: Srcsrc-1(RNAi) decreased the frequency of successful division in EMS (2/46 cells) compared with control(RNAi) (21/65 cells complete cytokinesis), while the frequency of successful division in P2 was unaffected (29/77 control(RNAi) P2 cells; 22/50 Srcsrc-1(RNAi) P2 cells divided successfully) (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: The frequency of successful division in P2 was unaffected by Srcsrc-1(RNAi) (29/77 control(RNAi) P2 cells; 22/50 Srcsrc-1(RNAi) P2 cells divided successfully) in formincyk-1(ts) mutant embryos.
claims.source: Srcsrc-1(RNAi) decreased the frequency of successful division in EMS (2/46 cells) compared with control(RNAi) (21/65 cells complete cytokinesis), while the frequency of successful division in P2 was unaffected (29/77 control(RNAi) P2 cells; 22/50 Srcsrc-1(RNAi) P2 cells divided successfully) (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: Srcsrc-1(RNAi) had no effect on the frequency of successful division in non-ts control embryos.
claims.source: Srcsrc-1(RNAi) had no effect on the frequency of successful division in non-ts control embryos (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The extrinsic mechanism protecting EMS cells from cytokinesis failure after inhibition of formincyk-1 is dependent on SrcSRC-1 signaling from P2 cells.
claims.source: Thus, the extrinsic mechanism protecting EMS cells from cytokinesis failure after inhibition of formincyk-1 is dependent on SrcSRC-1 signaling from P2 cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SrcSRC-1 RNAi data.

claims.claim: Both intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms modulate cytokinesis in individual blastomeres in the absence of robust F-actin levels in the contractile ring.
claims.source: Together, our data demonstrate that both intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms modulate cytokinesis in individual blastomeres in the absence of robust F-actin levels in the contractile ring.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Cell-type-specific differences were found in both the functional levels and temporal window of activity required for forminCYK-1 activity, but not myosin-IINMY-2 activity, during cytokinesis.
claims.source: We found cell-type-specific differences in both the functional levels and temporal window of activity required for forminCYK-1 activity, but not myosin-IINMY-2 activity, during cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: ForminCYK-1 inhibition resulted in cytokinesis failure in ABa and ABp blastomeres, similar to in the one-cell embryo.
claims.source: We found that, similar to in the one-cell embryo (Davies et al., 2014), forminCYK-1 inhibition resulted in cytokinesis failure in ABa and ABp blastomeres.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings and comparison to previous work.

claims.claim: Both EMS and P2 blastomeres were protected against cytokinesis failure and divided successfully with consistent frequency upon inhibition of forminCYK-1 and in the absence of a robust F-actin contractile ring.
claims.source: In contrast to the one-cell embryo and ABa/ABp cells, both EMS and P2 blastomeres were protected against cytokinesis failure and divided successfully with consistent frequency upon inhibition of forminCYK-1 and in the absence of a robust F-actin contractile ring.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Cytokinesis in EMS and P2 was more resistant to LatA than cytokinesis in ABa/ABp.
claims.source: This is not likely due to an F-actin-independent role for forminCYK-1, as we found cytokinesis in EMS and P2 was also more resistant to LatA, a pharmaceutical inhibitor of F-actin polymerization, than cytokinesis in ABa/ABp.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Cell isolation and blastomere pairing experiments revealed that P2 is protected against cytokinesis failure due to cell-intrinsic regulation and independent of contact with other blastomeres.
claims.source: Cell isolation and blastomere pairing experiments revealed that P2 is protected against cytokinesis failure due to cell-intrinsic regulation and independent of contact with other blastomeres.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: EMS is protected against cytokinesis failure by extrinsic regulation due to direct cell-cell contact with P2 and SrcSRC-1 mediated cell-fate signaling.
claims.source: In contrast, we found that EMS is protected against cytokinesis failure by extrinsic regulation due to direct cell-cell contact with P2 and SrcSRC-1 mediated cell-fate signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The early C. elegans four-cell embryo is established as a system to study cytokinetic diversity.
claims.source: This work establishes the early C. elegans four-cell embryo as a system to study cytokinetic diversity and suggests that, at least in the early C. elegans embryo, both cell-intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific cytokinetic diversity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the work presented.

claims.claim: At least in the early C. elegans embryo, both cell-intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific cytokinetic diversity.
claims.source: This work establishes the early C. elegans four-cell embryo as a system to study cytokinetic diversity and suggests that, at least in the early C. elegans embryo, both cell-intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific cytokinetic diversity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the work presented.

claims.claim: A 'normal', although F-actin-poor, contractile ring still forms in EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully in formincyk-1(ts) embryos at restrictive temperature.
claims.source: Although we could not detect enriched F-actin at the contractile ring in EMS or P2 in formincyk-1(ts) embryos at the restrictive temperature, we assume that a 'normal', although F-actin-poor, contractile ring still forms in the cells that divide successfully.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation that cells divide successfully despite undetectable F-actin enrichment.

claims.claim: In EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully upon forminCYK-1 inactivation, contractile ring constriction progresses more slowly.
claims.source: In EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully upon forminCYK-1 inactivation, contractile ring constriction progresses more slowly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these cells are utilizing a sub-optimal contractile ring.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: EMS and P2 cells are utilizing a sub-optimal contractile ring when forminCYK-1 is inactivated.
claims.source: In EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully upon forminCYK-1 inactivation, contractile ring constriction progresses more slowly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these cells are utilizing a sub-optimal contractile ring.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation that contractile ring constriction is slower.

claims.claim: MyosinNMY-2 is still essential for cytokinesis in EMS and P2.
claims.source: Indeed, myosinNMY-2 is still essential for cytokinesis in EMS and P2, indicating a 'normal' constricting actomyosin contractile ring is likely driving division in these blastomeres.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the myosin-IInmy-2(ts) data showing all cells fail in cytokinesis.

claims.claim: A 'normal' constricting actomyosin contractile ring is likely driving division in EMS and P2 blastomeres.
claims.source: Indeed, myosinNMY-2 is still essential for cytokinesis in EMS and P2, indicating a 'normal' constricting actomyosin contractile ring is likely driving division in these blastomeres.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation that myosinNMY-2 is essential.

claims.claim: EMS and P2 blastomeres are able to divide successfully with a substantially weakened F-actin contractile ring.
claims.source: Nonetheless, it is clear that, unlike one-cell embryos and ABa/ABp cells, EMS and P2 blastomeres are still somehow able to divide successfully with a substantially weakened F-actin contractile ring, whether weakened by inhibition of forminCYK-1 or application of low doses of Latrunculin A.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: EMS and P2 divide asymmetrically, whereas ABa and ABp divide symmetrically.
claims.source: An obvious distinction of these more robustly dividing cells is that EMS and P2 divide asymmetrically, whereas ABa and ABp divide symmetrically (Rose and Gönczy, 2014; Arata et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Anterior-posterior cell polarity and the PAR proteins are essential for robust cytokinesis in the one-cell C. elegans embryo.
claims.source: In the one-cell C. elegans embryo, we previously found that anterior-posterior cell polarity and the PAR proteins are essential for robust cytokinesis (Jordan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The PAR proteins localize to opposing cortical domains in P2 but are not obviously asymmetrically distributed in EMS.
claims.source: The PAR proteins localize to opposing cortical domains in P2 but are not obviously asymmetrically distributed in EMS (Arata et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arata et al., 2010.

claims.claim: In P2, cell polarity is cell-intrinsically established, though proper orientation of polarity relative to the spindle is dependent on cell-extrinsic signaling from EMS.
claims.source: Little is known about cell polarity establishment and/or maintenance in EMS, but in P2, cell polarity is cell-intrinsically established, though proper orientation of polarity relative to the spindle is dependent on cell-extrinsic signaling from EMS (Arata et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arata et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Whole embryo PAR protein disruption (by par-6(RNAi)) eliminates protection of cytokinesis in EMS and P2.
claims.source: While we found that whole embryo PAR protein disruption (by par-6(RNAi)) eliminates protection of cytokinesis in EMS and P2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), under these conditions, normal cell fate specification of the four-cell embryo is lost (Bowerman et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Bowerman et al., 1997.

claims.claim: Under par-6(RNAi) conditions, normal cell fate specification of the four-cell embryo is lost.
claims.source: While we found that whole embryo PAR protein disruption (by par-6(RNAi)) eliminates protection of cytokinesis in EMS and P2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), under these conditions, normal cell fate specification of the four-cell embryo is lost (Bowerman et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bowerman et al., 1997.

claims.claim: In mammalian cultured cells, traction-mediated cytofission, driven by daughter cell elongation, crawling, and cell-substrate adhesion, can promote cell division in the absence of an actomyosin contractile ring.
claims.source: In mammalian cultured cells, traction-mediated cytofission, driven by daughter cell elongation, crawling, and cell-substrate adhesion, can promote cell division in the absence of an actomyosin contractile ring (Choudhary et al., 2013; Wheatley et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cytofission.

claims.claim: Cytofission is not likely to be the main driver of cytokinesis in EMS and P2 cells.
claims.source: Cytofission is not likely to be the main driver of cytokinesis in these cells since, even upon blastomere isolation, we do not observe cell crawling behavior or increased daughter cell elongation in EMS or P2.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation that cell crawling and elongation are not observed.

claims.claim: Polar cortical relaxation is proposed to facilitate actomyosin contractile ring constriction at the cell equator by reducing cortical contractility outside of the division plane in the polar regions of the cell.
claims.source: Another possible driver of cytokinesis outside of the contractile ring is polar cortical relaxation, in which reduced cortical contractility outside of the division plane in the polar regions of the cell is proposed to facilitate actomyosin contractile ring constriction at the cell equator (Wolpert, 2014, 1960; Kunda et al., 2012; Rodrigues et al., 2015; Mangal et al., 2018; Lewellyn et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on polar cortical relaxation.

claims.claim: Polar cortical relaxation has been proposed to be regulated by Aurora A kinase activity, astral microtubules, and PP1-dependent phosphorylation of ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) family proteins.
claims.source: Polar cortical relaxation has been proposed to be regulated by Aurora A kinase activity, astral microtubules, and PP1-dependent phosphorylation of ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) family proteins (Kunda et al., 2012; Rodrigues et al., 2015; Mangal et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on polar cortical relaxation regulation.

claims.claim: Extrinsic cell fate signaling may have direct downstream effects on the cytokinetic machinery in EMS.
claims.source: In EMS, we found that cytokinesis is extrinsically protected and this protection is correlated with cell-fate signaling from P2. Thus, it is possible that extrinsic cell fate signaling has direct downstream effects on the cytokinetic machinery in EMS.

results.result: Cell-type-specific variation in the requirement for forminCYK-1, but not myosin-IINMY-2, was identified in four-cell C. elegans embryos. ABa and ABp cells are sensitive to forminCYK-1 inactivation, failing cytokinesis at restrictive temperatures, while EMS and P2 cells are resistant, successfully completing cytokinesis even at 26-27°C where ABa/ABp always fail.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C83 are supported by systematic temperature-shift experiments (Figure 1) showing differential cytokinesis outcomes across blastomeres. The data demonstrate that myosin-II inactivation causes similar failure rates in all four cells, while forminCYK-1 inactivation shows clear cell-type specificity with quantitative measurements at multiple temperatures. The experimental design includes appropriate controls and sufficient sample sizes (n≥5-81 per condition).

results.result: Temporal requirement analysis reveals that myosin-IINMY-2 is required throughout cytokinesis in all four blastomeres, while forminCYK-1 shows cell-type-specific temporal requirements. ABa requires forminCYK-1 throughout cytokinesis, ABp requires it only early, and EMS/P2 have lower overall requirements with successful division even when upshifted before anaphase onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C95 are supported by temporal upshift experiments (Figure 2) with temperature shifts at defined times relative to anaphase onset. The data show clear differences in temporal sensitivity between cell types with adequate sample sizes (n≥57-79 per condition). The conclusion that forminCYK-1-mediated actin dynamics underlie cytokinetic diversity (C95) is a reasonable inference from the combined functional and temporal data.

results.result: EMS and P2 cells have greatly reduced F-actin levels at the division plane upon forminCYK-1 disruption at restrictive temperature, yet still show considerable equatorial constriction and successful cytokinesis. This suggests these cells are less dependent on robust F-actin in the contractile ring and utilize cell-type-specific mechanisms for division.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 and C110-C115 are supported by F-actin imaging data using multiple reporters (Lifeact::RFP, PLST-1::GFP, GFP::UtrophinABD) shown in Figures 4 and supplements. The data demonstrate loss of F-actin enrichment at the contractile ring in all cells at 26°C in formincyk-1(ts) mutants, including in EMS/P2 cells that successfully divide. The inference that cell-type-specific mechanisms allow division without robust F-actin (C115) is well-supported by the combined observations.

results.result: Pharmacological inhibition of F-actin polymerization with LatrunculinA phenocopies the cell-type-specific requirement for forminCYK-1. ABa and ABp cells are sensitive to LatA treatment, while EMS and P2 cells are resistant, dividing at higher frequencies at the same LatA concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 and C116-C120 are supported by LatA dose-response experiments (Figure 5) showing cell-specific effects. At 80 nM LatA, 100% of ABa/ABp cells fail while ~25% of EMS/P2 cells successfully divide. This independent validation using a different perturbation method strengthens the conclusion that EMS/P2 are protected against cytokinesis failure when F-actin is weakened. Sample sizes are adequate (n=13-21 per condition).

results.result: Blastomere isolation experiments reveal that P2 cytokinesis is cell-intrinsically regulated, maintaining protection against forminCYK-1 disruption when isolated (~30% success rate). In contrast, EMS cytokinesis is cell-extrinsically regulated, with isolated EMS cells always failing cytokinesis (0/22 success) despite succeeding ~33% of the time in intact embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C121-C130 are supported by blastomere isolation experiments (Figure 6) with clear quantitative outcomes. The experimental design appropriately tests intrinsic vs. extrinsic regulation by removing cell-cell contacts. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10-26 per condition). The conclusion that P2 is intrinsically protected while EMS requires extrinsic signals is well-supported by the differential outcomes upon isolation.

results.result: Blastomere pairing experiments demonstrate that direct cell-cell contact from P2 is sufficient to restore cytokinetic protection in EMS. EMS cells paired with P2 divide successfully 16% of the time, while isolated EMS or EMS paired with ABd never divide. Increased EMS-P2 contact area correlates with successful EMS division, suggesting a link between P2-to-EMS signaling and cytokinetic protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 and C131-C140 are supported by blastomere pairing experiments (Figure 7) showing specific rescue of EMS cytokinesis by P2 contact. The correlation between contact area and division success (C137: p=0.0266) provides quantitative support, though the sample size for successful divisions is small (n=5). The inference of a correlation between signaling and division (C140) is reasonable but remains correlative rather than mechanistic.

results.result: EMS spindle orientation, a marker of successful P2-to-EMS signaling, correlates with cytokinesis outcome in formincyk-1(ts) mutants. In control EMS-P2 doublets, EMS spindles always align with the doublet axis (~180°). In formincyk-1(ts) doublets, only 48% show proper alignment, but all EMS cells that successfully divide (5/5) have properly aligned spindles. P2 cytokinesis outcome is independent of EMS spindle orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C148 are supported by spindle orientation analysis in paired blastomeres (Figure 8C). The data show clear correlation between proper spindle alignment and successful EMS division in formincyk-1(ts) mutants. The observation that all dividing EMS cells have proper alignment (5/5) is compelling despite small sample size. The independence of P2 outcomes from EMS spindle orientation supports cell-intrinsic regulation in P2. The suggestion of forminCYK-1 involvement in P2-EMS signaling (C145) is speculative but reasonable.

results.result: Cytokinesis in EMS is dependent on SrcSRC-1 signaling. RNAi depletion of SrcSRC-1 in formincyk-1(ts) embryos specifically decreases successful division in EMS (2/46 vs. 21/65 in controls) while not affecting P2 division frequency (22/50 vs. 29/77 in controls). SrcSRC-1 depletion has no effect in non-ts control embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C61 and C149-C152 are supported by SrcSRC-1 RNAi experiments (Figure 8D and supplement). The data show specific reduction in EMS cytokinesis success upon SrcSRC-1 depletion in the sensitized formincyk-1(ts) background, with no effect on P2 or in wild-type embryos. Sample sizes are adequate (n=29-77 per condition). This provides strong evidence that the extrinsic mechanism protecting EMS depends on SrcSRC-1 signaling.

results.result: ForminCYK-1::eGFP localizes to the division plane in all four blastomeres with similar peak cortical levels (maximum intensity projection). Sum intensity projection shows reduced total levels in EMS and P2 compared to ABa/ABp, but this does not support the hypothesis that resistance to forminCYK-1 inactivation is due to protein enrichment in EMS/P2.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 are supported by imaging of endogenous forminCYK-1::eGFP (Figure 3 and supplements). The maximum intensity projection data clearly show similar peak levels across all cells, while sum projection shows lower total levels in EMS/P2. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations of sum projection analysis in multicellular embryos. The conclusion that differential protein levels do not explain the phenotype (C109) is well-supported.

results.result: Two other formin-related genes (inft-2 and frl-1) are expressed at the four-cell stage, but none are significantly over-expressed in EMS or P2 relative to ABa/ABp. Individual RNAi depletion of six other formin-related proteins did not decrease cytokinesis failure frequency in any blastomere in formincyk-1(ts) mutants, suggesting no single formin compensates for forminCYK-1 loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are supported by transcriptional data citations and RNAi screen results (Figure 3—supplement 1). The negative results from the RNAi screen are appropriately interpreted as ruling out single formin compensation. The caveat that multiple formins might function together (C104) is appropriately acknowledged as speculation that cannot be ruled out by the data.

results.result: In EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully upon forminCYK-1 inactivation, contractile ring constriction progresses more slowly, suggesting use of a sub-optimal contractile ring. MyosinNMY-2 remains essential for cytokinesis in EMS and P2, indicating a 'normal' actomyosin contractile ring likely drives division, albeit with substantially weakened F-actin.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C167 are supported by kinetic analysis of ring constriction (Figure 2—supplement 1) and the myosin-II requirement data (Figure 1). The slower constriction in formincyk-1(ts) EMS/P2 cells supports the sub-optimal ring interpretation (C164). The continued requirement for myosin-II (C165) is strong evidence that an actomyosin ring still drives division (C166). The overall conclusion (C167) is well-supported by the combined data.

results.result: Both cell-intrinsic (P2) and cell-extrinsic (EMS) mechanisms control cytokinetic variation in individual cell types and can protect against division failure when the contractile ring is weakened. This work establishes the C. elegans four-cell embryo as a system to study cytokinetic diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C65, C153, and C161 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from multiple experimental approaches. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergent evidence from temperature-shift experiments, F-actin imaging, blastomere isolation/pairing, and SrcSRC-1 depletion. The establishment of the four-cell embryo as a model system is justified by the comprehensive characterization presented.

results.result: Background claims establishing that cytokinesis is powered by actomyosin ring constriction, that cytokinetic regulation has more diversity than previously appreciated, and that organism-wide mutations in cytokinesis genes cause cell-type-specific division defects in multiple organisms including humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C28 represent established knowledge and literature review supported by appropriate citations. These provide context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made, though verification of specific citation accuracy would require checking the original sources.

results.result: Background on C. elegans development and the four-cell embryo system, including cell lineage patterns, cell fate specification pathways, and the technical advantages of the system for studying cell-type-specific cytokinesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C44 represent established knowledge about C. elegans development supported by appropriate citations to classic studies and reviews. These provide essential background for understanding the experimental system but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Description of the temperature-sensitive mutants used: myosin-IInmy-2(ts) has a mutation in the neck domain affecting dimerization, while formincyk-1(ts) has a mutation in the FH2 domain affecting F-actin polymerization. Both mutations completely block cytokinesis in one-cell embryos at 26°C with null-like phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 and C66-C69 describe the experimental tools used, supported by citations to previous characterization studies (Davies et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2010). The characterization of these mutants as having null-like phenotypes at restrictive temperature is important for interpreting the results and is appropriately cited.

results.result: Background on formin function: diaphanous family formins are thought essential for contractile ring assembly and constriction. ForminCYK-1 is the only worm diaphanous family formin. In formincyk-1(ts) one-cell embryos, F-actin is present at 16°C but not visible at 26°C when cytokinesis fails.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 provide background on formin function and characterization of the formincyk-1(ts) mutant, supported by citations and data from Figure 1—supplement 1. This establishes the basis for using forminCYK-1 inactivation to study F-actin-dependent cytokinesis.

results.result: Discussion of potential mechanisms: EMS and P2 divide asymmetrically while ABa/ABp divide symmetrically. PAR proteins are essential for robust cytokinesis in one-cell embryos and localize asymmetrically in P2 but not obviously in EMS. PAR-6 RNAi eliminates cytokinetic protection in EMS/P2 but also disrupts normal cell fate specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C173 discuss potential mechanisms involving cell polarity. While the PAR-6 RNAi data (Figure 8—supplement 2) show loss of protection, the authors appropriately note that this result is confounded by loss of normal cell fate specification (C173), making it impossible to distinguish specific roles for PAR proteins in cytokinesis from indirect effects. The discussion is appropriately cautious but the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Discussion of potential mechanisms including cytofission, polar cortical relaxation, and cell fate signaling pathways (Wnt/Frizzled and RTK/Src). The authors note that cytofission is unlikely, discuss polar relaxation as a possibility, and present evidence linking cell fate signaling to cytokinetic protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C186 represent discussion and speculation about mechanisms. The dismissal of cytofission (C175) is supported by observations. The discussion of polar cortical relaxation (C176-C177) is speculative. The discussion of cell fate signaling (C178-C186) is supported by the correlation data and literature, but direct mechanistic evidence is limited. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future investigation rather than established findings.

results.result: Discussion of potential evolutionary advantages: P2 is in the germline lineage and inherits distinct factors. EMS and P2 are upstream of founder cell formation and undergo asymmetric divisions, potentially explaining why these cells have extra protection to ensure successful division and proper lineage specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C197 present speculative evolutionary explanations for the observed cytokinetic protection in EMS and P2. While the observations about lineage position and asymmetric division are factual (supported by established knowledge), the speculation about selective pressure and evolutionary advantage (C195, C197) represents reasonable hypotheses but lacks direct experimental support.

results.result: Prediction that similar regulation may contribute to cytokinetic variation in human cells and potentially mediate cell-type-specific pathologies, based on similarities between worm and human cell fate signaling and cytokinetic machinery.
results.evaluation: Claims C198-C199 represent speculative predictions about potential relevance to human biology. While the prediction is reasonable given the conservation of cytokinetic machinery and cell fate signaling pathways, it remains speculative without direct evidence in mammalian systems. This represents an appropriate discussion of potential broader implications.

results.result: Assumption that a 'normal' although F-actin-poor contractile ring still forms in EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully in formincyk-1(ts) embryos at restrictive temperature, despite inability to detect enriched F-actin.
results.evaluation: Claim C162 represents an assumption about what is happening in cells where F-actin cannot be detected but division succeeds. The authors acknowledge this is an assumption based on the observation that cells divide successfully. While reasonable given the myosin-II requirement, this remains an inference about undetectable structures rather than a directly supported observation.
